canonical_statement: The meta-analysis evaluated whether concomitant baseline MRA use was associated with differential cardiovascular effects of SGLT2 inhibitor therapy in heart failure regardless of ejection fraction.
The meta-analysis also evaluated MRA-associated adverse events among participants randomized to SGLT2 inhibitor therapy versus placebo.
The review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO as CRD42023397129.
PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and clinical trial registries were searched through 4 February 2023.
The search was restricted to English-language reports.
Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials or post-hoc RCT analyses enrolling adults with heart failure of any ejection fraction, with or without diabetes, and at least 6 months of follow-up.

population.label: Eligible adult heart-failure study population
inclusion_criteria: Heart failure regardless of ejection fraction

canonical_statement: Eligible comparisons randomized participants to an SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo and reported outcomes stratified by baseline MRA use.

population.label: Eligible randomized heart-failure trials
inclusion_criteria: Outcomes reported by baseline MRA use

canonical_statement: Observational studies, reviews, abstracts, animal studies, duplicate reports, and preprints were excluded.
Two investigators independently screened records and extracted data, with disagreements resolved through discussion and a senior investigator when required.
Risk of bias was assessed with the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials.

Hazard ratios or risk ratios were pooled with fixed-effect models using generic inverse-variance methods for time-to-event outcomes and Mantel-Haenszel methods for exploratory adverse-event comparisons.
Prespecified subgroup analyses examined baseline MRA use and heart-failure phenotype, and a sensitivity analysis excluded SOLOIST-WHF because sotagliflozin inhibits both SGLT1 and SGLT2.
Statistical heterogeneity was assessed with I² and publication-bias assessment included funnel-plot/Egger methods; analyses used Review Manager 5.4 and JASP 0.16.3.
Five eligible studies contributed data from 21,947 participants with heart failure, including 10,805 with type 2 diabetes.
The pooled evidence included 8,474 participants from HFrEF studies, 12,251 from HFpEF studies, and 1,222 from SOLOIST-WHF with diabetes and recent worsening heart failure.
Four included reports were post-hoc analyses of EMPEROR-Reduced, DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Preserved, and DELIVER, while SOLOIST-WHF provided the fifth trial dataset.
Where MRA type was reported, 79.0% of baseline MRA users received spironolactone, 20.9% eplerenone, and less than 0.1% canrenone.

population.label: Baseline MRA users in trials reporting MRA type

canonical_statement: Mean reported MRA doses were 31.4 mg for spironolactone and 32.5 mg for eplerenone.

population.label: Baseline MRA users in trials reporting dose

canonical_statement: Baseline MRA users were generally younger, had lower systolic blood pressure and lower ejection fraction, and more often had prior heart failure and NYHA class III/IV symptoms than non-users; renal function and background therapy also differed.
The randomized active treatments were dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, or sotagliflozin in the included heart-failure trials.

canonical_statement: In the exploratory comparison of MRA users versus non-users, the excess risk of mild hyperkalaemia was materially lower among SGLT2 inhibitor recipients than among placebo recipients (reported interaction P < 0.001 in the article text).
In the exploratory comparison of MRA users versus non-users, the interaction for severe hyperkalaemia was borderline (article text P = 0.051).
The authors concluded that baseline MRA use did not materially modify SGLT2 inhibitor effects on HHF/CVD, HHF, or all-cause mortality.

The authors interpreted the chronic-heart-failure cardiovascular-death subgroup as a possible greater relative benefit with concomitant MRA use, while emphasizing that the finding was hypothesis-generating.
The authors concluded that SGLT2 inhibitors appeared to attenuate MRA-associated treatment-emergent hyperkalaemia.
The authors called for adequately powered randomized trials to validate possible additive benefits of SGLT2 inhibitor and MRA therapy.
Participants were randomized to SGLT2 inhibitor therapy versus placebo, but baseline MRA use itself was not randomized.

The interaction analyses were not adjusted for multiple baseline variables, so observed differential SGLT2 inhibitor effects could reflect demographic, practice-pattern, or baseline-risk differences between MRA users and non-users.
Past MRA exposure was unavailable for participants who were not using an MRA at baseline.

The analysis did not account for MRA initiation or discontinuation during follow-up; adjusted hazard ratios and duration of differential MRA use were unavailable, limiting assessment of post-randomization bias.
Few HFrEF participants were not receiving an MRA at baseline, limiting power to detect interaction in that subgroup.
Definitions of composite kidney outcomes, volume depletion, and renal adverse events varied slightly across the included trials.

The proposed additive benefit of SGLT2 inhibitor plus conventional MRA therapy was explicitly hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation; additional data were identified as needed in patients with eGFR 30–45 mL/min/1.73 m².
